    The problem

    A network never tells you it broke.
    A person does, hours later.

    Nothing on a network announces itself. The disk fills quietly, the certificate lapses quietly, the new device joins quietly. What is not quiet is the phone call afterwards.

    • “The Wi-Fi has been weird since Tuesday.”
    • “Someone plugged something in. No idea what.”
    • “The certificate expired. On a Sunday, obviously.”
    • “The site was down four hours before anyone noticed.”

    Illustrative — the sentences a callout usually starts with, not quotes from named customers.

    Nobody can watch a network by hand at three in the morning. Something sitting on it, looking, can.

    What it watches

    One sensor on the network, one page with everything on it. No hunting through six different admin panels to answer one question.

    Who is on the network

    Every device that joins, every device that goes quiet, and the ones you have never seen before. Name the ones you recognise once and Vault stops asking about them.

    Your servers

    Disk, memory, load, and the updates waiting to be installed — including the ones that need a reboot before they count. You find out a disk is filling up while it is still a nuisance.

    Your websites and certificates

    Whether each site answers, how fast, and how many days are left on its certificate. An expiring certificate is a warning weeks out, not an outage on a Sunday.

    Where the traffic goes

    The names your devices look up, which ones were blocked, and which device asked. Useful when a smart TV is chatting to somewhere odd, and useful when something is broken and you need to know what it reached for.

    What is exposed, and who is knocking

    The ports actually reachable from outside, and the addresses trying them — where they are from and what they went after.

    Who is around

    Which phones and laptops are home, when they usually are, and how long they have been on today. The same signal answers "is anyone in the office?" and "how much estimated network presence was that?".

    How it works

    Three steps, and you are looking at your own network.

    1. Install the sensor

      One command on any machine that stays on — a spare Pi, a NAS, a server you already run. It watches from the inside, which is the only place a network is honest.

    2. It reports to the hub

      The sensor sweeps on a schedule and sends up a summary of what it found. Nothing else leaves the network: no packet captures, no file contents, no traffic tunnelled anywhere.

    3. You get a dashboard and an alert

      A single page for the whole picture, and a notification when something actually changes — a new device, a site down, a certificate running out, a port that opened. 

    curl -fsSL https://my.guarder.io/install | sh -s -- --code YOUR-ENROL-CODE

    The enrolment code comes from your own dashboard and is good for one sensor. Add a second network later and it gets its own.

    What it covers

    Six things that actually go wrong.

    Named the way a person would say them, with what Vault does about each.

    Malware and viruses

    Blocked

    A program that installs itself and then steals, spies, or quietly uses the machine for someone else.

    Known-bad domains are refused before anything can download from them or call home.

    Password guessing

    Blocked

    Somebody trying passwords over and over until one of them works.

    Repeated failures get the source banned at the machine, automatically.

    Known holes in software

    Fixed

    Published flaws in software you already run. Most break-ins use one of these, not anything clever.

    Security updates install in the window you choose, and Vault reports what changed.

    Fake networks

    Watched

    Somebody puts themselves between your devices and the internet — a fake Wi-Fi network, a second router — so everything you send passes through their hands.

    A new gateway, a second DHCP server or a rogue access point is flagged the moment it appears.

    Settings quietly changing

    Watched

    A setting that was protecting you gets switched off, and nobody notices for months.

    Vault keeps a baseline of the important settings and tells you the day one drifts.

    Expiring certificates

    Warned early

    The padlock on your website runs out and visitors get a full-page security warning.

    Every certificate it can read is watched, and you are warned weeks ahead with the steps to renew.

    The difference

    Every other tool sends you an alert.
    Vault sends you the repair it already made.

    An alert is only useful if someone acts on it, and at 2am nobody does. This is the part of Vault that is not a dashboard.

    A fixed list of repairs, not a shell

    Vault can restart a service that died, clear a log directory that filled a disk, install available package updates, or enable supported host protections. Certificate renewal depends on the host's configured tools. That list is fixed and allow-listed: if a repair is not on it, Vault cannot perform it, however it is asked.

    Every repair has a cooldown

    A fix runs, then that fix is locked for a while. A service that dies every ninety seconds gets restarted once and then escalated to you — because the second restart was never the answer, and a tool that keeps trying hides the real fault.

    Tell it what to do, in words

    There is an assistant on the dashboard that can read everything Vault knows and run those same repairs. Ask it why the office internet was slow last night, or tell it to restart the thing that is stuck.

    It asks first when it matters

    Anything disruptive — a reboot, cutting a device off the network — is proposed, not performed. You see exactly what it intends to do and say yes. Every action, automatic or asked for, is written down with who or what triggered it.

      Questions worth asking first

      What can the sensor actually see?

      What a device on your network can see by asking politely: which addresses answer and what hardware they claim to be, which ports on them are open, whether your sites and servers respond, and — if you point your DNS at Vault — the names that were looked up and by which device. It does not read your traffic, capture packets, or open files. On servers you connect it over your own SSH access and it runs read-only checks, plus exactly the repairs you allow.

      Where does the data live?

      In the hub for your account, and nowhere else — it is not sold, not pooled with anyone else's, and not used to train anything. What leaves your network is the sensor's summary of what it found, over HTTPS. Self-hosting the hub on your own machine is possible, and today it is something we set up with you rather than a download.

      What happens on my network if the hub is unreachable?

      Nothing. The sensor is not in the path of your traffic — it watches from the side, so if it stops, or the hub is down, or your uplink is out, your network carries on exactly as before. The sensor keeps sweeping and sends what it collected once it can reach the hub again. The one exception is DNS filtering, which is opt-in and only in the path if you choose to point your devices at it; it keeps answering from its own cache and lists, without the hub.

      What does it cost?

      Nothing for three months, and there is no card form anywhere on this site. There are no plans to choose between right now — tell us what you look after, we set the deployment up by hand, and you use the whole product. If that ever changes you will be told before it does, not after.

      How do I cancel?

      During the three months there is nothing to cancel: no card was taken and no plan was started. Tell us you are done and the deployment is removed; everything collected is yours to export first.
